claims.text: Differences in deformation and failure behavior between equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets are primarily caused by variations in lattice distortion and stacking-fault energy.
Variations in lattice distortion modify stacking-fault energy.
Stacking-fault energy alters the balance between dislocation slip and deformation twinning.
The quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy has stronger lattice distortion than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Stronger lattice distortion in the quinary alloy lowers its stacking-fault energy.
Lower stacking-fault energy promotes deformation-twin nucleation in addition to dislocation glide.
Enhanced twinning and work hardening give the quinary alloy superior tensile ductility and strength.
The quaternary and ternary alloys have higher stacking-fault energies than the quinary alloy.
The quaternary and ternary alloys nucleate fewer deformation twins than the quinary alloy.
Deformation of the quaternary and ternary alloys is more strongly dominated by dislocation slip than deformation of the quinary alloy.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower twin density.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower work-hardening rates.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys may have lower tensile ductility.
Using identical thermomechanical processing and comparable recrystallized grain sizes isolates intrinsic compositional effects.
The proposed comparison is restricted to single-phase FCC alloys with similar grain sizes and thermomechanical histories.
The proposed tests use room-temperature uniaxial tension in ambient air at a comparable strain rate of approximately 10^-3 s^-1.
Short-range ordering or processing-induced defects may also influence mechanical behavior.
